Secretary for Security Chris Tang said the national security law does not target any type of shop, "absolutely not." He pointed out that the national security law is a piece of legislation, and "regardless of whether you are a person or any type of company, if you break the law and there is evidence, I will arrest you; if there is sufficient evidence, I will prosecute you." He said it is not possible to arbitrarily target a certain profession or a certain shop, "I am targeting all lawbreakers and organisations."

"Just days after announcing its closure following the expiry of its lease on Tuesday (the 29th), the 50-year-old Tian Yuan Bookshop has now become embroiled in a national security case. Tian Yuan Bookshop and Leave a Bookstore (Lau Ye Bookstore) were raided by national security police on the 15th of this month, with arrests made. Three people from Leave a Bookstore and two from Tian Yuan Bookshop were arrested on suspicion of committing the offence of sedition under Article 23. Police said the five were suspected of violating Article 24 of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance — "acting with seditious intent" — and a batch of books was seized. It is understood that the books involved include 'Only Red Flowers Bloom: Identity and Belonging in the Era of Xi Jinping' by Feng Zheyun (Fung Chit-wan)."

On 29 June this year, Hunter Bookstore founder Wong Man-huen and her husband were arrested by national security police on suspicion of violating Article 23's offence of "acting with seditious intent," as well as money laundering and other charges.

Additionally, in March this year, One Punch Bookstore (Yat Kuen) operator Pong Yat-ming and three staff members were arrested by national security police. The four were accused of the Article 23 offence of "selling publications with seditious intent with knowledge," and books including a biography of Jimmy Lai were seized from the shop.
